title: From Practice to Field: A Multilevel Model of Practice-Driven Institutional Change
pub: Academy of Management Journal, Vol. 55, No. 4, pp. 877–904
author: Michael Smets · Tim Morris · Royston Greenwood

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess AI capability, verification or task selection directly, but materially extends the cluster’s operating-model argument by explaining how work redesign can emerge through local improvisation, then be coordinated, codified and diffused across an organisation and field. Its bounded, pre-generative-AI case supports a mechanism for institutional absorption rather than the cluster’s AI-specific empirical claims.
qs: We specify the role of the mundane yet pervasive  pressure to ‘get the job done’ as an underexplored origin of change and show the mechanisms by  which such practice-driven change emerges from day-to-day work, consolidates within the  organization, and may radiate to the level of the field to undermine the prevailing institutional logic.

In this sense,  coordination is the pulling together of distributed improvisations and their formalization into  policies and rules that describe and prescribe the new practice and, by implication, prioritize the  importance of one logic over another.

kp.k: Everyday legal work can generate institutional change
kp.d: This historical study does not examine AI. It develops a model explaining how adaptations in everyday professional work can consolidate within a firm and change field-level professional logics. The authors contrast this practice-driven pathway with explanations centred on external shocks, deliberate institutional entrepreneurship and overt contestation.
qs: This paper develops a model of practice-driven institutional change;
We emphasize how the struggle and noise typical of other theories of change are replaced by a relatively quiet and unobtrusive process of diffusion

kp.k: Evidence combines embedded observation, interviews and archival research
kp.d: The embedded case concerns Justitia, a pseudonymous global law firm formed through an Anglo-German merger in the early 2000s, and its English and German banking offices. The first author observed 42 participants, spending approximately 13 hours per working day for two weeks in each office. Evidence included 12 pilot interviews, 55 subsequent semi-structured interviews comprising 50 practitioner and five elite interviews, two day-long workshops, and firm and professional archival materials. Table 1 places observations in 2005 and formal and elite interviews in 2006; field-level evidence extends to the 2008 Legal Services Act.
qs: We drew upon three data sources: observation, interviews, and archival materials
In addition to the 12 pilot interviews, we conducted 55 semi-structured interviews
The observer also attended two day-long workshops.

kp.k: Cross-border transactions exposed competing professional logics
kp.d: The authors distinguish ideal-typical German fiduciary professionalism, oriented toward public service, judicial expectations and forensic analysis, from English expertise/client-service professionalism, oriented toward commercial advice and pragmatic problem-solving. Syndicated finance brought these approaches into direct contact: English-law loan agreements secured on German assets required cross-jurisdictional coordination to ensure enforceability. The study calls this interface 'germanizing'; its initial conflicts concerned both contract drafting and what counted as appropriate professional conduct.
qs: Their work is guided by an ideal-typical ‘expertise’ logic
German lawyers are predisposed to forensic analysis
In these discussions, German and English lawyers prioritized different critical audiences, based on their professional logic and training.

kp.k: Complexity, urgency and consequence jointly precipitate change
kp.d: The model identifies a combination of novel institutional complexity, tight deadlines and costly failure as the trigger for improvisation. At Justitia, client intolerance of inter-office disagreement and pressure to demonstrate seamless global service made inherited practices difficult to maintain. One observed partner warned that transaction failure would cost almost a million euros in fees. The authors distinguish novelty from longstanding complexity that organizations may already accommodate, and argue that complexity alone can instead produce polarization.
qs: It is the combination of these elements that constitutes a work-level crisis and thereby precipitates practice-driven institutional change.
Importantly, it is not the existence of institutional complexity per se that precipitates change, but the novelty of this complexity
transaction failure would lose the firm almost a million euros in fees.

kp.k: Mutual adaptation produced a client-oriented hybrid practice
kp.d: English lawyers introduced initial local-law due diligence and became more attentive to German legal constraints. German lawyers adopted more pragmatic approaches to achieving clients' intended outcomes while preserving enforceability under German law. Drafting combined comprehensive treatment of key terms with reliance on German statutes for less critical provisions. Although working methods drew from both jurisdictions, the authors argue that the resulting hybrid privileged client service rather than retaining equal weight for both professional logics.
qs: How do clients get to where they want to be – enforceable under German law?
think together to find out what is commercially wanted and how it can be legally implemented
The hybrid practice blended activities from both jurisdictions and introduced some new ones but, critically, oriented them towards realizing client interests.

kp.d: The mechanism of reorienting the normative network concerns whose expectations practitioners prioritize. German lawyers increasingly foregrounded clients, syndicate banks and rating agencies rather than courts. English colleagues justified this partly by their experience that carefully drafted private agreements reduced the likelihood of litigation. Client feedback reinforced the shift, criticizing academic debates, delays and poor coordination; reviews were understood to affect future assignments and career progress. The authors treat this justification as concurrent with improvisation, not a later campaign for external approval.
qs: They establish ‘who matters’ and, by implication, whose logic should apply.
These reviews, shared among all of the lawyers involved, were known to matter for the quality of future assignments and career progress.
It focuses on the justification of a solution, rather than the framing of a problem

kp.k: Firm coordination turns local experiments into shared routines
kp.d: Overlapping transaction teams circulated successful improvisations, while deadline pressure encouraged their reuse. Partners participating directly in service delivery identified and systematized these adaptations. An online comparison tool, inter-office secondments and a 2005 workshop codifying best-practice guidelines helped consolidate the emerging practice. The authors identify vertical connections between partners and frontline work and horizontal connections across teams as important enablers; the practice was not designed in advance by management.
qs: Partners, aware (and often creators) of the various practice-level improvisations, began to systematize them
Eventually, in 2005, a workshop was held to codify ‘best practice
the new hybrid practice, outlined in table 3, was not laid down at the outset

kp.k: Recruitment, feedback and status enable institutional distancing
kp.d: Institutional distancing shields practitioners from audiences enforcing established professional norms. The model identifies cosmopolitan recruitment, continuous positive feedback and status-based structural assurance as its supporting dynamics. International experience made recruits more receptive to alternative approaches; favourable reactions from clients, colleagues and partners amplified departures from inherited practice. Elite-firm status reassured lawyers and counterparties that unfamiliar practices were legitimate, while limited scrutiny from courts and regulators reduced countervailing feedback.
qs: Three interrelated dynamics underpin institutional distancing - cosmopolitanism, continuous positive feedback, and structural assurance
positive feedback encourages and escalates deviations from established norms, whereas negative feedback counteracts deviations.
new practices can gain legitimacy if they are associated with an elite firm.

kp.k: Transaction networks diffuse change without overt reform campaigns
kp.d: The authors describe unobtrusive embedding through repeated deals, document templates, syndication and interactions with other law firms. Syndication exposed additional banks and their lawyers to new documentation; clients also pressed competitors to adopt practices they preferred. Justitia's leading status supported acceptance. Unlike diffusion through public advocacy, this work-based pathway gave potential opponents limited visibility until changes were already embedded. This relative lack of contestation concerns field-level diffusion, not the absence of initial conflict between English and German colleagues.
qs: That’s how change creeps in.
We are influencing the market by our practices, which is making our competitors also need to change
Practice-driven change, in contrast, diffuses quietly – and without dramatic events – through the engagement of practitioners ‘doing work’.

kp.k: Regulatory endorsement followed changes already embedded in practice
kp.d: BRAK established its Working Party on International Law Firms in 2001, entered dialogue with international firms in 2005, and issued its report in 2007. The authors argue that limited resources and reliance on members' experience prevented detailed scrutiny of internal work. Legal challenges and concerns about preserving professional privileges made resistance harder. They interpret the report's accommodation of international firms and the 2008 Legal Services Act's emphasis on legal service as endorsement of a broader client-service logic, rather than as the original drivers of practice change.
qs: the enquiry did not penetrate to the working practices deep inside the international firms
In effect, the Report endorsed the client-service logic.
The Legal Services Act (2008) also endorsed the new logic by emphasizing the role of legal service to clients.

kp.k: Institutional change is neither fully strategic nor random
kp.d: The proposed mechanisms—situated improvising, reorienting the normative network and unobtrusive embedding—interact recursively. Practitioners intentionally solve immediate problems without necessarily intending to transform the profession. Shared tasks and repeated participation coordinate the accumulation of adaptations, while emerging legitimacy supports further departures. The authors consequently position practice-driven change between deliberate institutional redesign and accidental accumulation.
qs: The locus of change is the practice and the ‘entrepreneur’ is the practitioner at work.
Small changes in working practice are not unintentional, but motivated by the experience of novel institutional complexity.
Their accumulation is not accidental or random, but implicitly coordinated by their common purpose and connectedness through participation in practice.

kp.k: Generalization depends on organizational and historical conditions
kp.d: The authors explicitly limit their findings to professionals in one elite, merger-created international firm. They call for research across professions, jurisdictions and sectors, emphasizing historically contingent regulatory power. They suggest, rather than demonstrate, that more hierarchical organizations and tightly coupled sequential work may be less conducive to improvisation than participative partnerships and overlapping project teams. They also propose that practices co-produced by heterogeneous practitioners and demanding clients may be especially susceptible to adaptation.
qs: our findings have been derived from a study of professionals working within one organization, an elite international law firm created by merger.
the relative power of regulators and regulated may be historically contingent
More hierarchically structured organizations, in contrast, may be less accommodating of practice-level improvisations.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no claims about AI. Its own-domain claim is that everyday adaptations in cross-border legal work can accumulate into changes in professional practice and field-level institutional logic.
pts.d: Smets, Morris and Greenwood argue that pressure to complete transactions prompted English and German banking lawyers at the pseudonymous firm Justitia to develop a hybrid practice. English lawyers introduced initial local-law due diligence; German lawyers adopted more pragmatic, client-oriented problem-solving and blended drafting approaches. The authors identify three interacting mechanisms: situated improvising, reorienting the normative network, and unobtrusive embedding. They interpret the resulting German professional change as a shift from a fiduciary/public-service logic toward an expertise/client-service logic. Their further claim is that practices can diffuse through transactions, templates and professional interactions without a deliberate field-level reform campaign, making accumulated changes comparatively difficult to resist. These are findings and theoretical propositions about institutional change, not predictions of AI adoption or impact.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims derive from an embedded qualitative case study, triangulated with interviews, firm documents and German professional and legislative materials—not AI data or benchmarks.
pts.d: The authors studied the English and German offices of one international firm's banking group. Observation covered 42 participants, with approximately 13 hours per working day for two weeks in each office, plus two workshops. They conducted 12 pilot interviews and 55 subsequent semi-structured interviews, including five elite interviews. Internal contracts, transaction schedules, client reviews, training and best-practice materials supported the organizational account. Professional publications, the German Federal Bar's 2007 report and commentary on the 2008 Legal Services Act supported their interpretation of broader professional change. Interviewed lawyers described diffusion through reused transaction templates and client demands. The authors' claim about field-level change is an interpretation of this combined evidence, not a quantified causal estimate or evidence that Justitia alone caused legislative change.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account concerns internationalization from the 1990s through 2008; its broader propositions are conditional on work pressures, organizational arrangements and regulatory circumstances.
pts.d: Published in 2012, the study situates Justitia's merger in the early 2000s, observations and interviews principally in 2005–2006, codification of best practices in 2005, German Federal Bar endorsement in 2007, and legislative recognition in 2008. It offers no AI forecast or numerical timetable for future change. The proposed trigger is the joint experience of novel institutional complexity, urgency and consequential failure. Organizational coordination and institutional distancing amplify change through overlapping teams, senior practitioners' involvement, cosmopolitan recruitment, positive feedback and elite status. Low visibility and comparatively weak regulatory resistance condition unobtrusive diffusion. The authors explicitly limit generalization from one elite merged firm and suggest that hierarchical organizations, tightly coupled workflows or less heterogeneous practices may behave differently. Their account concerns norm-based changes that did not require prior authoritative ratification, rather than a general claim that binding legal rules can be changed through practice alone.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected participants are cross-border banking lawyers and their institutional clients; the authors trace wider consequences for competing firms, German professional identity and professional regulation.
pts.d: English solicitors adjust their workflows to German legal constraints, while German Rechtsanwälte increasingly orient advice and drafting toward commercial solutions and clients' expectations. Partners coordinate and legitimate changes; associates learn through transactions, overlapping teams, role models and feedback relevant to career progression. Banks, rating agencies and syndicate participants gain salience as referent audiences, while courts and professional bodies become less prominent in the practical evaluation of this work. Elite peer firms and midsize German firms encounter and adopt practices through transactions and client expectations. The authors interpret the German Federal Bar's response as accommodating international firms partly to protect collective professional privileges, whose loss would disproportionately affect smaller firms. The source does not claim AI-driven employment displacement, changes in staffing leverage, automated legal work or improved access to justice.
